Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

            - '\mshta.exe'

Miasma Phantom Gyp: python.exe (gyp parser) spawning node index.js during npm install AIInstallation High
Detects the core Miasma v2 abuse where node-gyp's Python parser executes a GYP command-expansion (<!(...)>) embedded in binding.gyp, spawning the credential-stealer payload as a child of python.exe rather than via package.json lifecycle hooks. Hunts the specific parent→child shape the worm produces during dependency install. Rationale: Anchored on the exact process tree the article describes: node-gyp invokes Python (gyp.py) to parse binding.gyp, and the embedded <!(node index.js > /dev/null 2>&1 && echo stub.c) command spawns node.exe with index.js as a direct child of python.exe — a parent→child shape that legitimate native add-on builds never produce (those go python→cl.exe/link.exe/cmake.exe). Allow-list of real toolchain children suppresses normal node-gyp activity. Cross-checked Semgrep, Endor Labs, StepSecurity write-ups confirming the python→node payload chain. Cross-checked against: • https://semgrep.dev/blog/2026/miasma-v2-self-spreading-npm-worm-now-uses-malicious-bindinggyp-file-and-compromises-57-packages/ • https://www.endorlabs.com/learn/malicious-payload-in-ai-sdk-ollama-npm-package • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/binding-gyp-npm-supply-chain-attack-spreads-like-worm • https://corgea.com/research/miasma-phantom-gyp-npm-worm-vapi-ai-sdk-ollama-june-2026
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.006 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate packages (e.g. node-pre-gyp, node-sass forks) where binding.gyp uses <!(node -e '...') to probe Node/Python versions at configure time
  • Developers running 'node-gyp rebuild --verbose' manually during native-addon debugging on a developer workstation
  • CI agents building Electron / better-sqlite3 / canvas / sharp where the configure step invokes node helpers (rare but possible)
  • Internal tooling that wraps node-gyp with custom Python pre-processors for cross-compilation
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("node-pre-gyp","--target_platform","--target_arch") and ProcessCommandLine has "-e" and ProcessCommandLine has "process.version")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull the full process tree (npm.cmd → node.exe → python.exe → matching child). Inspect the binding.gyp at the parent's working directory (look for <!(...), <!@(...), or pymod_do_main tokens); review the child's command line for 'index.js' or sandbox-escape Python literals. Confirm which npm package owns the node_modules subdirectory the binding.gyp came from. Step 2 — Contain: isolate the host from network, revoke any npm/GitHub/AWS/GCP/Azure/Vault tokens that resided on it (Miasma harvests all of these), force-rotate the developer's npm 2FA recovery codes, and pause CI runners using the same npm cache. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on InitiatingProcessAccountObjectId across DeviceFileEvents for reads of ~/.aws/credentials, ~/.ssh/id_rsa, ~/.npmrc, ~/.docker/config.json, ~/.config/gh/hosts.yml in the same window; check DeviceNetworkEvents for outbound to api.github.com / *.workers.dev from that node.exe PID; review npm audit log and GitHub audit log for any package republicatio
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","python3.exe","python","python3")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("gyp.py","node-gyp","binding.gyp","gyp_main")
| where FileName !in~ ("cl.exe","link.exe","cmake.exe","msbuild.exe","gcc.exe","g++.exe","clang.exe","clang++.exe","make.exe","nmake.exe","ld.exe","tracker.exe","rc.exe","cvtres.exe","mt.exe","conhost.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("node.exe","node","cmd.exe","sh","bash","dash","curl.exe","wget.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
   or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("index.js","__subclasses__","catch_warnings","echo stub.c","/dev/null 2>&1","__import__('os')","pymod_do_main")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("node_modules","npm-cache","_npx","yarn","pnpm") or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.cmd","npx.cmd","yarn.cmd","pnpm.cmd")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName matches regex @"(?i)[\\/]python3?(\.exe)?$"
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("gyp.py","node-gyp","binding.gyp","gyp_main")
| where not(ActingProcessName matches regex @"(?i)[\\/](cl|link|cmake|msbuild|gcc|g\+\+|clang|clang\+\+|make|nmake|ld|tracker|rc|cvtres|mt|conhost)\.exe$")
| where ActingProcessName matches regex @"(?i)[\\/](node|cmd|sh|bash|dash|curl|wget|powershell|pwsh)(\.exe)?$"
   or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("index.js","__subclasses__","catch_warnings","echo stub.c","/dev/null 2>&1","__import__('os')","pymod_do_main")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, SHA256
title: Miasma Phantom Gyp - Python gyp parser spawning Node payload via binding.gyp
id: 7f3b6c2a-d4e1-4a01-9c5e-3a4f1c8e7b22
description: Detects node-gyp's Python parser (gyp.py) spawning unexpected child processes during npm install, indicative of GYP command-expansion abuse used by the Miasma v2 / Phantom Gyp worm (June 2026)

  - Developers manually invoking node-gyp rebuild for native add-on debugging

Miasma-tainted package install: binding.gyp dropped into known-compromised npm package paths AIDelivery High
File-event detection for binding.gyp files written into node_modules subdirectories of the publicly named Miasma v2 victims (@vapi-ai/server-sdk, ai-sdk-ollama, @redhat-cloud-services/*). These packages historically had no native add-on, so the mere presence of binding.gyp inside their node_modules path is the campaign signature. Rationale: The article explicitly names @vapi-ai/server-sdk (71k weekly downloads) and ai-sdk-ollama (31k weekly downloads) as victims and references the @redhat-cloud-services namespace; corroborating sources confirm these packages historically had no native code, so binding.gyp inside their tree is the campaign signature. Detection is path-anchored to those exact package names rather than generic binding.gyp activity. Cross-checked Semgrep, Chainguard, and Endor Labs. Cross-checked against: • https://semgrep.dev/blog/2026/miasma-v2-self-spreading-npm-worm-now-uses-malicious-bindinggyp-file-and-compromises-57-packages/ • https://www.chainguard.dev/unchained/chainguard-artifacts-safe-from-miasma-phantom-gyp-npm-attack • https://www.endorlabs.com/learn/malicious-payload-in-ai-sdk-ollama-npm-package
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1505.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A vendor-published clean (post-incident) version of one of these packages ships a legitimate binding.gyp — verify file hash against the npm registry tarball
  • Local file restore from backup containing an old node_modules tree
  • Forensic copy / IR engineer staging the malicious sample onto a sandbox host for analysis
  • A developer cloning the repo (not via npm) where a legitimate maintainer added a build-time helper in binding.gyp
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: read the dropped binding.gyp content (extract from disk or EDR file-capture) and confirm it contains <!(...), <!@(...), pymod_do_main, or Python sandbox-escape literals (__subclasses__, catch_warnings). Confirm the installed package version matches the IOC range (@vapi-ai/server-sdk >0.11.0, ai-sdk-ollama >0.13.0). Step 2 — Contain: stop any in-flight node-gyp rebuild PID, isolate the host, and treat ALL credentials reachable from the host as burned — npm tokens, GitHub PATs, AWS/GCP/Azure CLI configs, kubeconfigs, Vault tokens, .npmrc auth. Trigger automated rotation. Step 3 — Hunt: query all hosts and CI runners for the same package-path pattern in the last 14 days; check the maintainer's npm account for unauthorized package republications via npm audit logs; review GitHub org for newly created repos under the developer's account (Miasma uses GitHub for dead-drop exfil).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName =~ "binding.gyp"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FolderPath has_any (
    @"node_modules\@vapi-ai\server-sdk",
    "node_modules/@vapi-ai/server-sdk",
    @"node_modules\ai-sdk-ollama",
    "node_modules/ai-sdk-ollama",
    @"node_modules\@redhat-cloud-services",
    "node_modules/@redhat-cloud-services")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("git.exe","code.exe","explorer.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FolderPath, FileName, FileSize, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "binding.gyp"
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFilePath has_any (
    @"node_modules\@vapi-ai\server-sdk",
    "node_modules/@vapi-ai/server-sdk",
    @"node_modules\ai-sdk-ollama",
    "node_modules/ai-sdk-ollama",
    @"node_modules\@redhat-cloud-services",
    "node_modules/@redhat-cloud-services")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSize, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine

Miasma payload SHA256 hash hit (published Phantom Gyp IOCs) AIInstallation Medium
Hash-based match for the four SHA256s associated with the Miasma v2 Phantom Gyp payload set. Fires on either file write or process execution telemetry. Universal IOC sweep across endpoint estate. Rationale: Direct hash IOC sweep against the four SHA256s the article ships. Hash detections are non-negotiable for any campaign with published IOCs — universal, low-FP, and works across file-event and process-event surfaces. Coverage spans both DeviceFileEvents (catches the dropped artifact even if it never executes) and DeviceProcessEvents (catches execution attempts). Cross-checked against: • https://semgrep.dev/blog/2026/miasma-v2-self-spreading-npm-worm-now-uses-malicious-bindinggyp-file-and-compromises-57-packages/
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Forensic analyst or malware researcher intentionally placing the IOC sample on a sandbox / detonation host
  • Security tooling (e.g. EDR test harness, YARA-rule unit test fixtures) staging the hash for validation
  • Threat-intel platform pre-caching the file for hash-lookup tests
  • Inbound email or chat attachment carrying the sample for IR analysis (will hit Defender mail scan first)
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in ("SOC-SANDBOX-01","IR-WORKSTATION-01","MALWARE-LAB-01")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: confirm the host is not a sanctioned forensic / sandbox / IR-analyst workstation by checking the device tag and the user's role in IdentityInfo. Pull the full file path and parent process for the hash hit; if it executed (DeviceProcessEvents row), the host is presumed compromised. Step 2 — Contain: isolate the device immediately via Live Response / Defender machine action, suspend the user's npm / GitHub / cloud sessions, kill the offending PID. Treat all secrets reachable from the host as burned and force rotation (npm tokens, GitHub PATs, AWS keys, .npmrc auth, kubeconfig, Vault tokens). Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on InitiatingProcessAccountObjectId and SHA256 across the full estate for the last 30 days; check whether any package on npm under the user's maintainer account was published in the same window (Miasma republishes from victim hosts); review GitHub audit log for new repos under the user's account in the last 7 days (potential dead-drop exfil endpoint).

Node child of node-gyp/python making outbound to GitHub dead-drop or anomalous web service during install AIexfil Medium
Catches the Miasma exfiltration step: after the binding.gyp command-expansion fires, the spawned node.exe (running index.js) beacons cloud credentials and CI tokens out to attacker-controlled GitHub repositories or webhook services. Pivots on the rare combination of node.exe with a node-gyp/python ancestor making outbound TCP to api.github.com, raw.githubusercontent.com, or first-seen external hosts. Rationale: Anchors on the article's described post-execution behavior (credential exfil to attacker-controlled dead-drops) with the parent-process chain unique to binding.gyp abuse. Corroborating sources (Endor Labs, Morphisec, OX Security) confirm Miasma exfils to GitHub dead-drop repos and uses Workers/webhook bouncers; this detection requires both the gyp ancestry AND the suspicious destination to fire, keeping FPs manageable while catching the campaign-specific exfil shape. Cross-checked against: • https://www.endorlabs.com/learn/malicious-payload-in-ai-sdk-ollama-npm-package • https://www.morphisec.com/blog/its-in-your-ai-assistant-now-shai-hulud-wave-3-and-the-miasma-worm-targeting-npm/ • https://www.ox.security/blog/600000-monthly-downloads-affected-miasma-supply-chain-attack-is-back-on-npm/
ATT&CKT1567.001 T1552.001 T1041
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate npm packages whose postinstall hook fetches assets from raw.githubusercontent.com (e.g. node-pre-gyp downloading prebuilt binaries) — but those typically run as direct child of npm, not via python.exe (gyp) chain
  • node-gyp packages that pull source tarballs from GitHub during configure step (rare; node-pre-gyp uses HTTP downloader)
  • CI runners that genuinely push to api.github.com via node-based GitHub API client called from a build hook
  • Cloudflare Workers used by an org's internal build accelerator service
Suppression filter
| where not (ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("node-pre-gyp","prebuild-install") and DstHostname has "objects.githubusercontent.com")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull the spawning binding.gyp content and the node process's full argv; identify which npm package owns the source path. Check whether the GitHub destination repo is org-controlled (legitimate) or an externally owned account (likely dead-drop). Step 2 — Contain: kill the node.exe PID, isolate the device, and immediately rotate every credential reachable from the host — focus first on the developer's GitHub PAT (worm publishes via it), npm publish token, AWS keys in ~/.aws/credentials, .npmrc auth, kubeconfig, Vault tokens, GCP/Azure CLI cache. Step 3 — Hunt: query GitHub audit log for new repository creations under the developer's user account in the last 24h (Miasma creates ephemeral dead-drop repos); search ImNetworkSession for any other node.exe egress to the same destination from CI runners in the last 7 days; check npm registry for unauthorized package publications under the dev's maintainer accounts.
let gyp_node_children = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where FileName =~ "node.exe"
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","python3.exe","cmd.exe","sh","bash")
    | where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("gyp.py","binding.gyp","node-gyp")
        or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("python.exe","python3.exe")
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project ProcSpawnTime=Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessId, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe"
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("api.github.com","raw.githubusercontent.com","objects.githubusercontent.com",".workers.dev","webhook.site","ngrok.io","hooks.slack.com","discord.com/api/webhooks","transfer.sh","file.io","0x0.st")
   or RemoteIPType == "Public"
| join kind=inner gyp_node_children on DeviceId, $left.InitiatingProcessId == $right.ProcessId
| where Timestamp between (ProcSpawnTime .. ProcSpawnTime + 5m)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, ProcessCommandLine=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, GypParentCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine1
| order by Timestamp desc
let gyp_node_children = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where ActingProcessName matches regex @"(?i)[\\/]node(\.exe)?$"
    | where ParentProcessName matches regex @"(?i)[\\/](python3?|cmd|sh|bash)(\.exe)?$"
    | where ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("gyp.py","binding.gyp","node-gyp")
    | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
    | project ProcSpawnTime=TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActingProcessId, ParentProcessCommandLine;
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstHostname has_any ("api.github.com","raw.githubusercontent.com","objects.githubusercontent.com",".workers.dev","webhook.site","ngrok.io","hooks.slack.com","discord.com","transfer.sh","file.io","0x0.st")
| join kind=inner gyp_node_children on DvcHostname
| where TimeGenerated between (ProcSpawnTime .. ProcSpawnTime + 5m)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcUsername, DstHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkBytes, ParentProcessCommandLine
source:(windows.sysmon OR crowdstrike) @EventID:3 @Image:(*\\node.exe OR *\\Node.exe OR *\\NODE.EXE) (@DestinationHostname:(*api.github.com* OR *raw.githubusercontent.com* OR *.workers.dev OR *webhook.site* OR *ngrok.io* OR *hooks.slack.com* OR *discord.com* OR *transfer.sh* OR *file.io* OR *0x0.st*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\node\.exe$/i ParentBaseFileName=/^(python3?|cmd|sh|bash)\.exe$/i ParentCommandLine=/(gyp\.py|binding\.gyp|node-gyp)/i
| join({#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/(api\.github\.com|raw\.githubusercontent\.com|objects\.githubusercontent\.com|\.workers\.dev$|webhook\.site|ngrok\.io|hooks\.slack\.com|discord\.com|transfer\.sh|file\.io|0x0\.st)/i}, field=aid, include=[DomainName, ContextImageFileName])
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, DomainName, CommandLine, ParentCommandLine], function=count())

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="node.exe" AND Processes.parent_process_name IN ("python.exe","python3.exe","cmd.exe","sh","bash") AND (Processes.parent_process="*gyp*" OR Processes.parent_process="*binding.gyp*" OR Processes.parent_process="*node-gyp*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_id Processes.process_name Processes.parent_process Processes._time | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | rename _time as proc_time process_id as suspect_pid | join type=inner dest suspect_pid [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.dest="api.github.com" OR All_Traffic.dest="raw.githubusercontent.com" OR All_Traffic.dest="*.workers.dev" OR All_Traffic.dest="*.webhook.site" OR All_Traffic.dest="*.ngrok.io" OR All_Traffic.dest="hooks.slack.com" OR All_Traffic.dest="discord.com") AND All_Traffic.app="node.exe" by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.app | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | rename src as dest dest as net_dest app as suspect_pid]
Suspicious browser extension installation Installation Medium
Side-loaded / unsigned extensions, often masquerading as wallets, productivity tools.
ATT&CKT1176
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry DeviceRegistryEvents
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where RegistryKey has_any ("\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\","\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\","\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where RegistryKey has_any (@"\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\",
                              @"\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\",
                              @"\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryKey,
          RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Browser Extension Installation via Registry
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0a
status: experimental
description: |
    Registry writes under the browser extension policy keys —
    administrative install of an extension. Often used by adware /
    info-stealers to bypass user-level extension controls.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1176/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1176
    - attack.persistence
logsource:
    category: registry_event
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetObject|contains:
            - '\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\'
            - '\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\'
            - '\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - Group-policy-managed extension whitelists
level: medium

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

ImFileEvent

title: Crypto-Wallet Keystore Access by Non-Wallet Process
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d02
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers / wallet drainers read keystore files from MetaMask,
    Exodus, Atomic, Phantom, Bitcoin, Electrum, Ethereum-cli wallets.
    Filtering out the legitimate wallet binaries leaves only attacker
    activity.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1005/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1005
    - attack.collection
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Ethereum\keystore\'
            - '\Bitcoin\'
            - '\Exodus\'
            - '\Electrum\wallets\'
            - '\MetaMask\'
            - '\Phantom\'
            - '\Atomic\Local Storage\'
    filter_legit:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\MetaMask.exe'
            - '\Exodus.exe'
            - '\Atomic.exe'
            - '\electrum.exe'
            - '\Bitcoin.exe'
            - '\Phantom.exe'
    condition: selection_path and not filter_legit
falsepositives:
    - Backup software
level: high
ENDPOINT

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Bitcoin\wallet.dat"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Exodus\exodus.wallet*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Electrum\wallets\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\MetaMask\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Phantom\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Atomic\Local Storage\*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("MetaMask.exe","Exodus.exe","Atomic.exe","electrum.exe","Bitcoin.exe","Phantom.exe")

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Ethereum\keystore\*"

PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High
Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"

ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

SecurityEvent

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("ef641e956f91d501b748085996303c96a64d67f63bfeef0dda175e5aa19cca90", "288f26c2eadcb1a7923fe376d16f5404216cce15d9fc162a4a78574dc7df399a", "e3dbe63aded45278f49c4746ab938ed9472b36def79b43e2dd2d7eff014481d1", "ceff7c51d70832c3ec8dd2744b606a23b3c924ef664ae23439b9b742ea154108") or SHA1 in~ ("ef641e956f91d501b748085996303c96a64d67f63bfeef0dda175e5aa19cca90", "288f26c2eadcb1a7923fe376d16f5404216cce15d9fc162a4a78574dc7df399a", "e3dbe63aded45278f49c4746ab938ed9472b36def79b43e2dd2d7eff014481d1", "ceff7c51d70832c3ec8dd2744b606a23b3c924ef664ae23439b9b742ea154108") or MD5 in~ ("ef641e956f91d501b748085996303c96a64d67f63bfeef0dda175e5aa19cca90", "288f26c2eadcb1a7923fe376d16f5404216cce15d9fc162a4a78574dc7df399a", "e3dbe63aded45278f49c4746ab938ed9472b36def79b43e2dd2d7eff014481d1", "ceff7c51d70832c3ec8dd2744b606a23b3c924ef664ae23439b9b742ea154108")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("ef641e956f91d501b748085996303c96a64d67f63bfeef0dda175e5aa19cca90", "288f26c2eadcb1a7923fe376d16f5404216cce15d9fc162a4a78574dc7df399a", "e3dbe63aded45278f49c4746ab938ed9472b36def79b43e2dd2d7eff014481d1", "ceff7c51d70832c3ec8dd2744b606a23b3c924ef664ae23439b9b742ea154108") or SHA1 in~ ("ef641e956f91d501b748085996303c96a64d67f63bfeef0dda175e5aa19cca90", "288f26c2eadcb1a7923fe376d16f5404216cce15d9fc162a4a78574dc7df399a", "e3dbe63aded45278f49c4746ab938ed9472b36def79b43e2dd2d7eff014481d1", "ceff7c51d70832c3ec8dd2744b606a23b3c924ef664ae23439b9b742ea154108") or MD5 in~ ("ef641e956f91d501b748085996303c96a64d67f63bfeef0dda175e5aa19cca90", "288f26c2eadcb1a7923fe376d16f5404216cce15d9fc162a4a78574dc7df399a", "e3dbe63aded45278f49c4746ab938ed9472b36def79b43e2dd2d7eff014481d1", "ceff7c51d70832c3ec8dd2744b606a23b3c924ef664ae23439b9b742ea154108")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["ef641e956f91d501b748085996303c96a64d67f63bfeef0dda175e5aa19cca90", "288f26c2eadcb1a7923fe376d16f5404216cce15d9fc162a4a78574dc7df399a", "e3dbe63aded45278f49c4746ab938ed9472b36def79b43e2dd2d7eff014481d1", "ceff7c51d70832c3ec8dd2744b606a23b3c924ef664ae23439b9b742ea154108"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")

| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host

| order by files desc

| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")

            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("52fda5c1b9704544f32ee98d9060e689", "51d39aa39478beeac94f2d12f682ecce") or SHA1 in~ ("52fda5c1b9704544f32ee98d9060e689", "51d39aa39478beeac94f2d12f682ecce") or MD5 in~ ("52fda5c1b9704544f32ee98d9060e689", "51d39aa39478beeac94f2d12f682ecce")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("52fda5c1b9704544f32ee98d9060e689", "51d39aa39478beeac94f2d12f682ecce") or SHA1 in~ ("52fda5c1b9704544f32ee98d9060e689", "51d39aa39478beeac94f2d12f682ecce") or MD5 in~ ("52fda5c1b9704544f32ee98d9060e689", "51d39aa39478beeac94f2d12f682ecce")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["52fda5c1b9704544f32ee98d9060e689", "51d39aa39478beeac94f2d12f682ecce"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB

    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"

     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")

Node-gyp Supply Chain Compromise: A Self-Propagating npm Worm That Hides in binding.gyp

Snyk
2026-06-04 11 use cases 4 techniques 7 kill-chain phases detected

A new npm worm is abusing binding.gyp to trigger node-gyp during install, letting malicious packages run code without lifecycle scripts. It steals credentials, persists in GitHub, and self-propagates across maintainers.

Phantom Gyp: node-gyp install-time code execution via weaponized binding.gyp AIExploitation High
Hunts the Miasma/Phantom Gyp install-time execution primitive where a malicious binding.gyp uses gyp command substitution (<!(node index.js > /dev/null 2>&1 && echo stub.c)) to run node index.js during npm install with no preinstall/postinstall hook. Anchors on the exact, byte-identical shell string shipped in @vapi-ai/server-sdk@1.2.2 and autotel@3.4.3. Rationale: Anchors on the byte-for-byte 157-byte binding.gyp payload string '<!(node index.js > /dev/null 2>&1 && echo stub.c)' quoted verbatim in the Snyk write-up and confirmed by StepSecurity's 'Phantom Gyp' analysis — the 'echo stub.c' + 'index.js' pairing has no benign equivalent. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/binding-gyp-npm-supply-chain-attack-spreads-like-worm • https://socprime.com/active-threats/miasma-supply-chain-attack-spreads-through-the-phantom-gyp-worm/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/binding-gyp-supply-chain-attack-compromises-dozens-of-npm-packages/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate native addon whose binding.gyp coincidentally runs a helper named index.js (rare; would not also echo stub.c)
  • Internal build tooling that pipes a node script to /dev/null during CI configure steps
  • Security researchers detonating the sample in a sandbox
  • Developer testing a custom gyp command-expansion build step
Suppression filter
| where not (ChildCmd has "node-sass" or ChildCmd has "\\test\\fixtures\\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ChildCmd and ParentCmd; confirm the parent chain is npm/node-gyp and the command contains both 'index.js' and 'echo stub.c'. Identify the package directory under node_modules and the package@version. 2) Contain: isolate the host/CI runner, kill the node process tree, and treat any npm/GitHub/AWS/GCP/Azure/Vault/Kubernetes credential reachable from that context as compromised — rotate immediately. 3) Hunt: search the same host for the Bun download (UC2), .github/workflows injection (UC3), and the loader hashes (UC4); enumerate other hosts that installed the affected package versions via lockfiles.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "index.js" and ProcessCommandLine has "stub.c"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "echo stub.c" or (ProcessCommandLine has "/dev/null" and ProcessCommandLine has "index.js")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "index.js" and TargetProcessCommandLine has "stub.c"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "echo stub.c" or TargetProcessCommandLine has "/dev/null"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          ParentProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine,
          TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Miasma loader fetches standalone Bun v1.3.13 from oven-sh GitHub releases during install AIInstallation High
Hunts the Miasma second-stage loader that, after binding.gyp triggers index.js, downloads a standalone Bun v1.3.13 binary from the official oven-sh/bun GitHub releases via curl and unzips it to a temp dir to run the next stage. Anchors on the hardcoded release URL path. Rationale: The Snyk decode of the 907-byte first decrypted blob quotes the literal URL template 'https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/releases/download/bun-v1.3.13/bun-<os>-<a>.zip'; the pinned 'bun-v1.3.13' release path inside a curl/install context is a high-fidelity, low-noise anchor. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/binding-gyp-npm-supply-chain-attack-spreads-like-worm • https://socprime.com/active-threats/miasma-supply-chain-attack-spreads-through-the-phantom-gyp-worm/
ATT&CKT1105 T1608.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer legitimately installing Bun v1.3.13 via curl for a real project
  • CI pipeline that provisions Bun as a build dependency
  • Dockerfile build step pulling that exact Bun release
  • Mirror/proxy cache warmers fetching the oven-sh release artifact
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("docker.exe","dockerd","buildkitd")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parent process is node/npm (not an interactive shell or Dockerfile RUN) and check whether index.js / binding.gyp execution (UC1) preceded it on the same host within minutes. 2) Contain: isolate the host/runner, block egress to the temp-dir Bun binary, kill the process tree, and rotate all reachable cloud/CI credentials. 3) Hunt: inspect the temp directory for the unzipped bun binary, look for subsequent credential-file reads (~/.npmrc, ~/.aws, ~/.config/gcloud, kube config, Vault tokens) and outbound GitHub API calls used for exfil.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "oven-sh/bun/releases/download/bun-v1.3.13"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "oven-sh/bun/releases/download/bun-v1.3.13"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          ParentProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Miasma GitHub Actions workflow injection for persistence by node payload AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the Miasma worm injecting GitHub Actions workflow files (.github/workflows/*.yml) for persistence, written by a node/npm process rather than a developer's editor. Targets the persistence step that lets the worm re-trigger and re-exfiltrate from CI. Rationale: The article and StepSecurity both state the worm 'injects GitHub Actions workflows for persistence'; constraining the writer to node/npm/bun (the install-time payload host) separates worm injection from a developer authoring workflows in an editor. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/binding-gyp-npm-supply-chain-attack-spreads-like-worm • https://cybersecuritynews.com/binding-gyp-supply-chain-attack-compromises-dozens-of-npm-packages/
ATT&CKT1546 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A scaffolding tool (e.g. a generator run via node) legitimately creating .github/workflows during project init
  • Yeoman/create-* CLIs writing CI templates
  • A node-based codemod that rewrites workflow files in bulk
  • Renovate/Dependabot-style automation editing workflows locally
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "create-" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "yo "
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the written workflow yaml — look for steps that exfiltrate env/secrets, curl to attacker GitHub repos, or re-run the install payload; correlate with UC1/UC2 on the same host. 2) Contain: revert/remove the injected workflow, revoke the repo's Actions tokens and any GITHUB_TOKEN/PAT, and rotate cloud secrets stored as Actions secrets. 3) Hunt: enumerate all repos the compromised maintainer account can push to for the same injected workflow, and review recent npm publish events from that account.

| where FolderPath has "\\.github\\workflows\\" or FolderPath has "/.github/workflows/"
| where FileName endswith ".yml" or FileName endswith ".yaml"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","node.exe","npm","npm.cmd","bun","bun.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has "/.github/workflows/" or TargetFilePath has "\\.github\\workflows\\"

| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","npm","bun")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Miasma/Node-gyp loader file hashes present on developer or CI host AIDelivery Medium
Alerts on any of the seven published Miasma loader SHA256 (and SHA1) hashes appearing as a written or executed file on endpoints/CI runners. Direct IOC match for the obfuscated index.js loader chain from the Node-gyp Supply Chain Compromise - June 2026. Rationale: Uses the seven SHA256 and three SHA1 hashes pre-extracted from the article (the Miasma loader chain); a direct hash hit is unambiguous TP and requires no behavioral inference. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/binding-gyp-npm-supply-chain-attack-spreads-like-worm • https://snyk.io/blog/node-gyp-supply-chain-compromise-self-propagating-npm-worm-binding-gyp/
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel/sandbox host intentionally storing the sample for analysis
  • SOAR enrichment that downloads the IOC file for sandboxing
  • Backup/AV quarantine copy of the same file re-hashed on a second host
  • Hash collision (negligible for SHA256)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the file path and the npm package@version it belongs to (node_modules/...); confirm whether it was merely written or also executed (correlate with UC1). 2) Contain: isolate the host/runner, delete/quarantine the file, and rotate every credential reachable from that host (npm, GitHub, AWS, GCP, Azure, Vault, Kubernetes). 3) Hunt: pivot on the package versions named in the Snyk advisory (@vapi-ai/server-sdk 0.11.1/0.11.2/1.2.1/1.2.2, ai-sdk-ollama, autotel 2.26.4/3.4.3, awaitly 1.33.3) across all lockfiles and CI caches in the estate.

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002

logsource:
    category: process_creation

detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")

Package manager runtime connecting to durabletask/axios supply-chain C2 IOCs AICommand & Control High
Network connections from node/python/npm/pip processes to the C2 IPs and domains attributed to the March 2026 axios npm hijack and May 2026 durabletask Python backdoor. Pivots on the article's exact infrastructure observables so it survives binary renaming and code refactors. Rationale: Anchors on the article's exact C2 IPs (142.11.206.73, 160.119.64.3) and domains (sfrclak.com, check.git-service.com, t.m-kosche.com, packages.npm.org typosquat of packages.npmjs.org). Initiating process scoping to node/python/npm/pip turns this from a flat IOC sweep into a supply-chain-specific signal that distinguishes the malicious-package-postinstall pattern from a workstation browsing.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1195.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal package mirror reverse-proxied through the same IP range (rare; verify by ASN)
  • Security researcher sandbox replaying IOCs against test hosts
  • Misconfigured npm config pointing to packages.npm.org typo unrelated to the campaign
  • Threat-intel ingestion pipeline that resolves the IOCs for enrichment
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files\\InternalMirror\\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree for the alerting host — what package (npm/pip) installation kicked off the node/python that egressed? Confirm whether the host is a dev workstation or CI runner. 2) Contain: isolate the host via Defender Live Response; rotate any cloud credentials (AWS/Azure/GCP/K8s/Vault) sourced from that host in the last 14 days; quarantine the offending package version from the internal registry. 3) Hunt: search Defender DeviceNetworkEvents and DNS logs across the org for the same IPs/domains over 30 days; pivot on the parent package name in npm/pip audit logs to enumerate every host that installed it; review CloudTrail/AzureActivity for AssumeRole/STS or kubectl exec from those hosts.
