Lateral movement via aws ssm send-command or kubectl exec spawned by python/node AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the durabletask post-compromise tradecraft — backdoored Python (or its node equivalent) shelling out to aws/kubectl to spread laterally using the victim's own credentials via SSM SendCommand/StartSession or kubectl exec. The parent-runtime pivot is what makes this article-specific rather than a generic admin-tool detection. Rationale: The article specifies the durabletask backdoor spread 'to other instances over SSM and to other pods via kubectl exec' using the victim's own credentials. Filtering AWS/kubectl execution to a python/node parent makes this an actual supply-chain signal rather than admin-tool noise, and the CloudTrail variant catches the same activity by user-agent footprint when EDR isn't on the host.
ATT&CKT1021.007 T1609 T1078.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Python-based CI orchestrator (Ansible, custom build scripts) legitimately running aws ssm send-command against fleet
  • Boto3-driven SSM automation for patch management
  • Kubernetes operators (written in Python/Go served by node) routinely exec'ing into pods
  • Developer using Boto3 in a Jupyter notebook to debug SSM run-commands
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("ansible","\\salt\\","\\jenkins\\","\\gha-runner\\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the originating package — pull npm/pip install history and DeviceProcessEvents for the python/node parent's full ancestry; confirm the package matches durabletask or a known-bad supply-chain release. 2) Contain: revoke the IAM role / kubeconfig the runtime used (rotate STS, invalidate kubeconfig tokens); isolate the host; snapshot to forensic storage before reboot. 3) Hunt: search CloudTrail for every SSM SendCommand / StartSession originating from the compromised role across the org window; enumerate target instances and pull EDR on each; in K8s, audit kube-apiserver logs for exec verbs from the same ServiceAccount and walk the affected pods.

| where FileName in~ ("aws.exe","aws","kubectl.exe","kubectl")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("ssm send-command","ssm start-session","kubectl exec","exec -it","exec --stdin")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("python","python3","node","python.exe","python3.exe","node.exe")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("aws","aws.exe","kubectl","kubectl.exe")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("ssm send-command","ssm start-session","kubectl exec","exec -it","exec --stdin")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Downloader or shell child of npm/pip install (postinstall RAT loader) AIInstallation Medium
Detects the axios-style postinstall pattern where a malicious package's install hook reaches out for a second-stage payload via curl/wget/powershell/bitsadmin. The parent-equals-package-manager pivot turns generic downloader behavior into a supply-chain-specific signal. Rationale: The axios hijack 'added one new dependency whose only job was a postinstall script that pulled down a cross-platform RAT and deleted itself' — the loader behaviour is a download from a non-language-runtime binary spawned by the package manager. Parent==package-manager + child==downloader + URL/download-cmdline is the article's exact shape.
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.001 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • node-gyp / native-module build pulling source archives via curl during install
  • Python wheels with C extensions running curl to download CMake/MSBuild prerequisites
  • pnpm/yarn fetching tarballs from a private registry that resolves through curl-based postinstall scripts
  • Corporate npm proxy doing legitimate token fetches via PowerShell
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("node-gyp","prebuild-install","cmake-js"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full process tree (npm/pip → downloader → ?) and the downloaded URL; query the org for every host that installed the same package@version. 2) Contain: quarantine the package version in the internal registry; pull the host offline; revoke any tokens that touched the registry. 3) Hunt: search DeviceFileEvents for files written by the downloaded process within ±10 minutes of the alert; pivot to DeviceNetworkEvents for any subsequent connections; enumerate other developer machines that ran the same package install over the last 30 days.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.exe","pip.exe","pip3.exe","node.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","npm","pip","pip3","yarn","pnpm")
| where FileName in~ ("curl.exe","wget.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","bash","sh","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("http://","https://","Invoke-WebRequest","DownloadString","-OutFile","/dev/tcp/","base64 -d")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("npm","pip","pip3","node","python","python3","yarn","pnpm")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("curl","wget","powershell","pwsh","bitsadmin","certutil","bash","sh")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("http://","https://","Invoke-WebRequest","DownloadString","-OutFile","/dev/tcp/","base64 -d")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\npm.exe OR *\NPM.EXE OR *\pip.exe OR *\PIP.EXE OR *\pip3.exe OR *\node.exe OR *\NODE.EXE OR *\python.exe OR *\PYTHON.EXE OR *\python3.exe OR *\yarn.exe OR *\pnpm.exe) @Image:(*\curl.exe OR *\CURL.EXE OR *\wget.exe OR *\powershell.exe OR *\PowerShell.exe OR *\pwsh.exe OR *\bitsadmin.exe OR *\certutil.exe) @CommandLine:(*http* OR *Invoke-WebRequest* OR *DownloadString* OR *-OutFile*)

Cloud credential file access by node/python runtime AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the durabletask second-stage credential harvest where a backdoored Python (or node) runtime reads .aws/credentials, .azure, .kube/config, gcloud config, .vault-token, and .npmrc. Targets the file paths the article enumerates — AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, Vault. Rationale: The article states the durabletask second stage 'harvested credentials from AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, and Vault'. The standard paths for those credential stores (~/.aws/credentials, ~/.kube/config, ~/.azure, ~/.config/gcloud, ~/.vault-token, ~/.npmrc) being touched by node/python is the concrete behaviour. The runtime filter keeps this from firing on AWS CLI / kubectl / az themselves.
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1528
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Boto3-based deploy scripts legitimately reading ~/.aws/credentials for SDK auth
  • Python K8s client (kubernetes-client) loading ~/.kube/config on startup
  • Pulumi/CDK programs written in Python/TypeScript reading multi-cloud creds during deploy
  • Azure SDK for Python loading cached ~/.azure tokens
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("aws-sdk","boto3-sts-refresh","pulumi","cdk deploy","kubernetes-client"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: examine the parent of the node/python process — was it spawned by npm/pip install? Identify the package; pull the file's hash and check VirusTotal/threat intel. 2) Contain: rotate every cloud credential touched (AWS access keys, Azure refresh tokens, GCP service-account keys, Vault tokens, npm publish tokens); revoke kubeconfig context tokens; isolate the host. 3) Hunt: search CloudTrail/AzureActivity/GCP audit for use of those credentials from new IPs in the last 14 days; query DeviceNetworkEvents for the host's outbound connections after the file access to identify exfil destination; pivot on the package name across the org install logs.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","node","python","python3")
| where FolderPath has_any (@".aws\credentials", ".aws/credentials", @".kube\config", ".kube/config", @".azure\", "/.azure/", "/.config/gcloud/", @"\gcloud\", ".vault-token", ".npmrc")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, FileName, FolderPath, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","node","python","python3")
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@".aws\credentials", ".aws/credentials", @".kube\config", ".kube/config", @".azure\", "/.azure/", "/.config/gcloud/", @"\gcloud\", ".vault-token", ".npmrc")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Locale-conditional rm -rf wiper command from python/node runtime AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the durabletask wiper logic — a one-in-six destructive rm -rf /* invoked from a Python/Node interpreter on hosts with Israeli or Iranian locale. The rm -rf /* + python/node parent combination is the article's exact tradecraft. Rationale: The article states: 'On hosts with Israeli or Iranian locale settings, a one-in-six roll ran rm -rf /*'. The parent==python/node + cmdline==`rm -rf /*` combination is the literal article-specific impact behavior — extremely high signal because a developer never legitimately wipes their own root.
ATT&CKT1485 T1561.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Docker container init script that legitimately runs `rm -rf /tmp/*` during cleanup (regex anchored to root prevents this)
  • Dockerfile build steps spawned from a Python orchestrator that include destructive cleanup of build artifacts
  • Test harness for filesystem code that intentionally invokes the command in a sandbox
  • Misconfigured CI cleanup job using --no-preserve-root for non-root directory wipes
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("docker build","buildx","kaniko","Dockerfile"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: this is critical — page the on-call analyst immediately. Confirm whether the command executed successfully (check for filesystem damage, host responsiveness). Identify the package that introduced the python/node parent. 2) Contain: isolate the host and any peers that received SSM/kubectl exec from it; snapshot the disk for forensics before any restore; quarantine the package version across the registry. 3) Hunt: search the org for every host that installed the same package@version and any process tree containing the rm command; pull locale settings (LANG/LC_*) from those hosts to identify which were targeted; check for the article's IOCs (142.11.206.73, 160.119.64.3, sfrclak.com) on the same hosts to confirm campaign attribution.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","python3.exe","node.exe","python","python3","node")
| where FileName in~ ("rm","sh","bash","busybox","dash")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\brm\s+-rf\s+(/\*?|--no-preserve-root)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("python","python3","node","python.exe","python3.exe","node.exe")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\brm\s+-rf\s+(/\*?|--no-preserve-root)"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: rm -rf Wiper Spawned from Python/Node Runtime
id: 2a8d6e7f-93c1-4b50-8e2f-c47a9d1b35e0
status: experimental
description: Detects the durabletask backdoor wiper logic — a destructive rm -rf /* spawned from a Python or Node interpreter (one-in-six probability on hosts with Israeli/Iranian locale per the article).
references:
  - https://www.aikido.dev/blog/edr-proxy-wont-protect-supply-chain-malware
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/03
tags:
  - attack.t1485
  - attack.t1561.001
  - attack.impact
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '/python'
      - '/python3'
      - '/node'
  cmdline:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'rm -rf /*'
      - 'rm -rf /'
      - 'rm -rf --no-preserve-root'
  condition: parent and cmdline
level: critical
(source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.command_line:("rm -rf /*" OR "rm -rf /" OR "rm -rf --no-preserve-root")) OR (source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @CommandLine:(*"rm -rf /*"* OR *"rm -rf /"* OR *"--no-preserve-root"*) @ParentImage:(*\python.exe OR *\python3.exe OR *\node.exe OR *\PYTHON.EXE OR *\NODE.EXE))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/(python3?|node)(\.exe)?$/i ImageFileName=/^(rm|sh|bash|busybox|dash)$/i
| regex("\\brm\\s+-rf\\s+(/|--no-preserve-root)", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("python","python3","node","python.exe","python3.exe","node.exe") AND Processes.process_name IN ("rm","sh","bash","busybox","dash") AND (Processes.process="*rm -rf /*" OR Processes.process="*rm -rf /" OR Processes.process="*rm -rf --no-preserve-root*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("python","python3","node","python.exe","python3.exe","node.exe") AND Processes.process_name IN ("rm","sh","bash","busybox","dash") AND (Processes.process="*rm -rf /*" OR Processes.process="*rm -rf /" OR Processes.process="*rm -rf --no-preserve-root*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium

        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["069ac1dc7f7649b76bc72a11ac700f373804bfd81dab7e561157b703999f44ce", "7d80b3ef74ad7992b93c31966962612e4e2ceb93e7727cdbd1d2a9af47d44ba8", "3de04fe2a76262743ed089efa7115f4508619838e77d60b9a1aab8b20d2cc8bf", "aeaf583e20347bf850e2fabdcd6f4982996ba023f8c2cd56bbd299cfd56516f5", "85f54c089d78ebfb101454ec934c767065a342a43c9ee1beac8430cdd3b2086f", "877ff2531a63393c4cb9a3c86908b62d9c4fc3db971bc231c48537faae6cb3ec", "c0b094e46842260936d4b97ce63e4539b99a3eae48b736798c700217c52569dc", "2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Multiple redhat-cloud-services npm Packages compromised

StepSecurity
2026-06-02 10 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Several packages in the @redhat-cloud-services npm scope were found to carry malicious payloads that fire via a preinstall hook on every npm install. The affected versions span multiple packages across the RedHat Cloud Services frontend ecosystem. The payload is a sophisticated multi-stage credential harvester that targets GitHub Actions secrets, AWS, GCP, Azure, Kubernetes, HashiCorp Vault, npm tokens, and CircleCI tokens

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Bun runtime download to /tmp from a node process during npm install · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Multiple redhat-cloud-services npm Packages compromised
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] npm preinstall hook executing oversized node index.js from @redhat-cloud-services package · [LLM] Bun spawned from npm install context executing /tmp/p*.js implant
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Process reading /proc/<pid>/mem of GitHub Actions Runner.Worker (in-memory secret extraction)
npm preinstall hook executing oversized node index.js from @redhat-cloud-services package AIInstallation High
Detects the entry point of the @redhat-cloud-services supply-chain compromise: a preinstall script firing node against an unusually large (>1 MB) index.js shipped inside an @redhat-cloud-services scoped package directory. The legitimate libraries in this scope have tiny entry files, so a 4.2 MB index.js executing during install is a near-deterministic signal of the malicious version. Rationale: Anchors on the exact preinstall execution string named in package.json (`node index.js`) combined with the scoped-package path `@redhat-cloud-services` and the article's distinguishing 4.2 MB size of index.js (vs <100 KB for legitimate releases). Cross-checked against the StepSecurity disclosure and the three RedHatInsights GitHub issues (#492, #2329, #57). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/RedHatInsights/javascript-clients/issues/492 • https://github.com/RedHatInsights/frontend-components/issues/2329 • https://github.com/RedHatInsights/platform-frontend-ai-toolkit/issues/57
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate RedHat dev tooling installs on engineer workstations once a clean version is republished — pin to the known-malicious versions in the affected-packages table
  • Internal mirrors that proxy the registry may still serve a cached malicious tarball after upstream removal
  • Security-team-controlled detonation sandboxes installing the bad versions intentionally for IR
  • CI re-runs from cached node_modules tarballs that pre-date the cleanup
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("--dry-run","--ignore-scripts") or ProcessCommandLine has "--ignore-scripts")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: confirm the installed package@version against the affected-packages table (e.g. host-inventory-client@5.0.3, types@3.6.1); pull the on-disk index.js size and SHA256; correlate with the GitHub Actions run / developer workstation identity. Step 2 — Contain: kill the node process; quarantine the host's node_modules; rotate every secret the host had access to (AWS, GCP, Azure, GitHub PATs, npm tokens, Vault, CircleCI, Kubernetes kubeconfigs); revoke OIDC-issued tokens minted during the window. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on UC2/UC3/UC4 for the same host; search registry-mirror access logs for the malicious versions being pulled by other workloads; review GitHub branch-protection bypass and any commits signed by the same OIDC identity during the install window.
let SuspectPackages = dynamic(["@redhat-cloud-services/types","@redhat-cloud-services/frontend-components-utilities","@redhat-cloud-services/frontend-components","@redhat-cloud-services/rbac-client","@redhat-cloud-services/javascript-clients-shared","@redhat-cloud-services/frontend-components-config-utilities","@redhat-cloud-services/frontend-components-notifications","@redhat-cloud-services/tsc-transform-imports","@redhat-cloud-services/frontend-components-config","@redhat-cloud-services/eslint-config-redhat-cloud-services","@redhat-cloud-services/host-inventory-client","@redhat-cloud-services/rule-components","@redhat-cloud-services/notifications-client","@redhat-cloud-services/chrome","@redhat-cloud-services/hcc-pf-mcp"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm","npm.exe","node","node.exe","yarn","pnpm","npx","npm-cli.js")
| where FileName in~ ("node","node.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "@redhat-cloud-services" and ProcessCommandLine has "index.js"
| extend MatchedPackage = tostring(set_difference(SuspectPackages, dynamic([])))
| join kind=leftouter (
    DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
    | where FolderPath has "@redhat-cloud-services" and FileName =~ "index.js"
    | where FileSize > 1048576
    | summarize MaxSize = max(FileSize) by DeviceId, FolderPath
) on DeviceId
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, MaxSize, MatchedPackage
| order by Timestamp desc
let SuspectScope = "@redhat-cloud-services";
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where Facility in ("user","daemon","kern") or ProcessName in ("auditd","audispd")
| where SyslogMessage has "node" and SyslogMessage has SuspectScope and SyslogMessage has "index.js"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("preinstall","npm install","npm-cli.js","npx","yarn","pnpm")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostName, Facility, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: npm preinstall executes oversized index.js from @redhat-cloud-services
id: 4f8a3c2d-9e1b-4a7c-8f60-1b9d2e3c4a51
description: Detects node executing an index.js inside a @redhat-cloud-services scoped package directory during npm install, the entry point of the June-2026 supply-chain compromise.
references:
  - https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/multiple-redhat-cloud-services-npm-packages-compromised
author: SOC Detection Eng
date: 2026/06/01
tags:
  - attack.initial_access
  - attack.t1195.002
  - attack.execution
  - attack.t1059.007
logsource:
  category: process_creation
detection:
  parent_selection:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '/npm'
      - '/node'
      - '/yarn'
      - '/pnpm'
      - '\npm.exe'
      - '\node.exe'
  child_selection:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/node'
      - '\node.exe'
  cmdline_selection:
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - '@redhat-cloud-services'
      - 'index.js'
  condition: parent_selection and child_selection and cmdline_selection
level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.command_line:(*node*@redhat-cloud-services*index.js* OR *Node*@redhat-cloud-services*index.js*) AND (@process.parent.name:(npm OR node OR yarn OR pnpm OR npx) OR @process.command_line:(*preinstall* OR *"npm install"*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/\/(node|node\.exe)$/i
| ParentBaseFileName=/^(npm|node|yarn|pnpm|npx)(\.exe)?$/i
| regex("@redhat-cloud-services", field=CommandLine)
| regex("index\\.js", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName], function=count())

Bun runtime download to /tmp from a node process during npm install AIDelivery High
Detects Stage 3 of the redhat-cloud-services compromise: the in-memory _b downloader retrieves bun-v1.3.13 from the official Bun GitHub releases CDN and drops it into a randomly-named /tmp/ subdirectory, then registers it via globalThis.getBunPath. Article-specific because legitimate library installs never fetch a parallel JS runtime at install time. Rationale: Anchors on the article's exact runtime version `bun-v1.3.13`, the GitHub releases CDN host (`objects.githubusercontent.com` is the actual blob host behind github.com release downloads), and the `/tmp/<random>/bun` drop path described in Stage 3. Pairs network event with the file-create within 5 minutes to suppress generic Bun installs on developer machines. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/releases/tag/bun-v1.3.13
ATT&CKT1105 T1036.005
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer manually running curl/bun installer to try Bun on a workstation
  • CI image-build steps that legitimately download Bun for a project that uses it (rare in RHEL/insights tooling)
  • Renovate/Dependabot autodeps tasks that exercise package install in sandboxes
  • Sysadmin troubleshooting a previously-cached corrupt Bun binary
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("package.json\"bun\"","bunfig.toml") or DeviceName has_any ("-bunlab-","-bunci-"))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: confirm the parent of the node download is an npm install of an @redhat-cloud-services package; capture the URL, the dropped /tmp/<random>/bun, and its SHA256. Step 2 — Contain: kill node, the Bun process, and any /tmp/p*.js it spawned; isolate the host; revoke any cloud / GitHub OIDC tokens issued to the runner. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot to UC3 (/proc/<pid>/mem reads by Bun) and UC4 (Bun executing /tmp/p*.js); look across the fleet for any other host that fetched bun-v1.3.13 from a node process — every hit is a likely-compromised CI runner.
let BunDownload = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","node.exe","npm")
    | where (RemoteUrl has "github.com/oven-sh/bun/releases" or RemoteUrl has "bun-v1.3.13" or RemoteUrl has "objects.githubusercontent.com")
    | project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP;
let BunDrop = DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
    | where ActionType == "FileCreated"
    | where FolderPath startswith "/tmp/" or FolderPath startswith "/var/folders/"
    | where FileName in~ ("bun","bun.exe")
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","node.exe","tar","unzip")
    | project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine;
BunDownload
| join kind=inner BunDrop on DeviceId
| where Timestamp1 between (Timestamp .. Timestamp + 5m)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, DropPath = strcat(FolderPath, FileName), InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
let BunNet = ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
    | where (Url has "github.com/oven-sh/bun/releases" or Url has "bun-v1.3.13" or DstHostname has "objects.githubusercontent.com")
    | where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","npm")
    | project NetTime = TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, Url, DstIpAddr;
let BunDrop = ImFileEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
    | where EventType == "FileCreated"
    | where TargetFilePath startswith "/tmp/" or TargetFilePath startswith "/var/folders/"
    | where TargetFileName in~ ("bun","bun.exe")
    | project DropTime = TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName;
BunNet
| join kind=inner BunDrop on DvcHostname
| where DropTime between (NetTime .. NetTime + 5m)
| project NetTime, DropTime, DvcHostname, Url, DstIpAddr, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by NetTime desc

| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName, DomainName], function=count())

Process reading /proc/<pid>/mem of GitHub Actions Runner.Worker (in-memory secret extraction) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the credential-harvesting core of the implant: reading /proc/<pid>/mem of the GitHub Actions Runner.Worker process to scrape secrets that the runner holds in memory but never writes to disk. This is exactly the activity the StepSecurity Harden-Runner screenshot in the article captured and is the technique the payload uses to evade Harden-Runner-style detections by reading rather than calling out. Rationale: Anchors on /proc/<pid>/mem — the exact /proc read the article's Harden-Runner process-events screenshot captures — combined with node/bun as the reader (the Stage 1 entry point and the Stage 3 downloaded runtime). Joins forward to DeviceProcessEvents on the target PID to confirm it is Runner.Worker, eliminating debugger / strace noise. Source: StepSecurity blog + image SCR-20260601-oxms.png in-article screenshot showing Runner.Worker /proc/mem read. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/007/ • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/multiple-redhat-cloud-services-npm-packages-compromised
ATT&CKT1003.007 T1552.001 T1212
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Node-based debugger or profiler legitimately attached to a worker for performance work
  • Systemd-coredump or abrt-hook-ccpp reading process memory during a crash dump (different parent, usually root-owned)
  • Custom observability agent written in node that reads /proc to monitor RSS (verify by image hash / installed-package source)
  • SRE running strace -p / gdb -p against the runner during incident response
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("gdb","strace","perf record","abrt-hook-ccpp","systemd-coredump") or AccountName == "root" and InitiatingProcessFileName == "systemd-coredump")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull the InitiatingProcessCommandLine and parent tree of the node/bun reader; confirm the target PID is Runner.Worker by joining to process-create events; capture /tmp/<random>/bun SHA256. Step 2 — Contain: kill the node and bun processes; isolate the runner; revoke the runner's GitHub Actions OIDC tokens and every workflow secret the job had access to (GITHUB_TOKEN, AWS_*, GCP_*, AZURE_*, NPM_TOKEN, VAULT_TOKEN, CIRCLE_TOKEN, KUBECONFIG); rotate any long-lived keys downstream actions chained to. Step 3 — Hunt: search the fleet for any other process reading /proc/<pid>/mem of Runner.Worker (different package may share the same TTP); review last 30 days of GitHub Actions secret usage from those workflows; audit all artifacts produced by jobs that ran this implant.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("FileOpened","FileAccessed","FileCreated")
| where FolderPath startswith "/proc/" and FileName == "mem"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","bun")
| extend TargetPid = extract(@"/proc/(\d+)/", 1, FolderPath)
| join kind=leftouter (
    DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
    | where FileName has_any ("Runner.Worker","Runner.Listener")
    | project DeviceId, TargetPid = tostring(ProcessId), RunnerCmd = ProcessCommandLine, RunnerName = FileName
) on DeviceId, TargetPid
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, TargetPid, RunnerName, RunnerCmd
| order by Timestamp desc
let ProcMemRe = @"/proc/\d+/mem";
let RunnerHits = Syslog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
    | where SyslogMessage matches regex ProcMemRe
    | where SyslogMessage has_any ("node", "bun")
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostName, Facility, ProcessName, SyslogMessage;
let AsimHits = ImFileEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
    | where TargetFilePath matches regex ProcMemRe
    | where ActingProcessName has_any ("node", "bun")
    | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath;
union isfuzzy=true RunnerHits, AsimHits
| order by TimeGenerated desc

#event_simpleName=/^(FileOpenInfo|FileWritten)$/

Bun spawned from npm install context executing /tmp/p*.js implant AIInstallation High
Detects Stage 3→4 handoff: the freshly downloaded /tmp/<random>/bun binary executes a randomly-named /tmp/p<random>.js file containing the AES-decrypted main payload. Combination of Bun residing in /tmp/, being invoked by a node process whose CWD is inside an npm install, and immediately running a /tmp/p*.js is article-specific and effectively never benign. Rationale: Anchors on three article-specific shapes that compose into a near-zero-FP signal: Bun binary path under /tmp/<random>/bun (Stage 3 drop), parent in (node, npm, bun) (Stage 1 / Stage 3 chain), child commandline matching /tmp/p<random>.js (Stage 4 implant file). Each alone is noisy; together they reproduce the Stage 3→4 handoff in the StepSecurity write-up. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/multiple-redhat-cloud-services-npm-packages-compromised • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1140/
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1140 T1620
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer hand-running `bun /tmp/playground.js` from a tutorial — different filename shape, won't match /tmp/p<random>.js
  • CI cache step that materialises a build artifact under /tmp/p* and runs it (verify by parent process and signed-by metadata)
  • Node test-runner that uses ephemeral /tmp files but with deterministic names (jest-*, mocha-*) — won't match the p<random> pattern
  • Renovate/dependency-update sandbox using its own tarball install — typically not Bun-mediated
Suppression filter
| where not (AccountName == "root" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("systemd","snapd")) and not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--test","--inspect","jest","mocha"))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: capture full process tree (npm → node → bun chain), the SHA256 of /tmp/<random>/bun and /tmp/p<random>.js; preserve both files for IR. Step 2 — Contain: kill bun and any child it spawned; isolate the host / runner; revoke every workflow secret + every cloud token (AWS / GCP / Azure / GitHub OIDC / npm / Vault / CircleCI / Kubernetes) the runner had access to; tear down the runner VM rather than reuse. Step 3 — Hunt: dump and reverse /tmp/p<random>.js to identify the C2 domain (article notes the B5 cipher with password ba2c6ddb3672bdd6a611e6850b4f700b52aed3dab2f1b3d5f8c839d4a157a709 and salt 5b26508dc0f1075a7c0b4d8aa464487e — once decrypted, sweep DNS for that domain); pivot to UC2/UC3 hits on the same host; audit GitHub Actions runs for all affected packages.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where (FolderPath startswith "/tmp/" and FileName in~ ("bun","bun.exe")) or (InitiatingProcessFolderPath startswith "/tmp/" and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("bun","bun.exe"))
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","node.exe","npm","bun")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"/tmp/p[A-Za-z0-9]+\.js"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
let TmpJsRe = @"/tmp/p[A-Za-z0-9]+\.js";
let AsimHits = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
    | where (ActingProcessName endswith "/bun" or ActingProcessName endswith "/node" or ActingProcessName endswith "/npm")
    | where TargetProcessCommandLine matches regex TmpJsRe or ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex TmpJsRe
    | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine;
let SyslogHits = Syslog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
    | where SyslogMessage matches regex TmpJsRe
    | where SyslogMessage has_any ("bun", "node")
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostName, ProcessName, SyslogMessage;
union isfuzzy=true AsimHits, SyslogHits
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: 9e1b4a7c-8f60-1b9d-2e3c-4a517c1b9d2e
description: Detects the redhat-cloud-services Stage 4 implant pattern — Bun binary located in /tmp executing /tmp/p<random>.js, invoked from a node/npm parent.
references:

source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE ((@process.executable.path:/tmp/*/bun AND @process.command_line:*/tmp/p*.js*) OR (@process.parent.name:(node OR npm OR bun) AND @process.command_line:(*/tmp/bun*/tmp/p*.js* OR *bun */tmp/p*.js*)))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| (ImageFileName=/^\/tmp\/[^\/]+\/bun$/i OR ParentBaseFileName=/^bun$/i)
| ParentBaseFileName=/^(node|npm|bun)$/i
| regex("\\/tmp\\/p[A-Za-z0-9]+\\.js", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName], function=count())

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]

    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user

| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"

Laravel-Lang Supply Chain Attack: Every Tag Across Multiple Composer Packages Rewritten to Steal CI Secrets

StepSecurity
2026-06-02 9 use cases 2 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

On May 22, 2026, an attacker with push access to the Laravel-Lang GitHub organization rewrote every git tag across multiple popular Composer packages within a single 15 minute window. Anyone running composer update or installing fresh against laravel-lang/http-statuses, laravel-lang/actions, or laravel-lang/attributes now pulls a payload that exfiltrates CI secrets to a typosquatted attacker domain. StepSecurity confirmed end to end exploitation in an isolated runner and has filed security issues in all four repositories.

ATT&CKT1190 T1195.002
Domainsflipboxstudio.info
SHA1a5ea2e8fa92ccf29… 50ac0db454d19234… c45764e70285146d… a9f8d88cf98e3598… bba2e443dc7ff1f8…

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] GitHub bulk git tag force-push by single actor across multiple org repos
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] PHP CLI drops hidden /tmp dropper artefacts (Laravel-Lang autoload payload) · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Laravel-Lang Supply Chain Attack: Every Tag Across Multiple Composer Packages Re
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Egress to typosquatted C2 flipboxstudio.info (Laravel-Lang Composer SC) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Orphaned process (ppid=1) executing from /tmp hidden hex path (post-dropper stage-2)
Egress to typosquatted C2 flipboxstudio.info (Laravel-Lang Composer SC) AICommand & Control High
Hunts DNS or HTTP(S) callbacks to flipboxstudio.info, the attacker-controlled typosquat of the legitimate flipboxstudio.com used as the stage-1 fetch endpoint (/payload) and stage-2 exfiltration sink (/exfil) by the May 2026 Laravel-Lang Composer supply-chain dropper. Single-IOC alerter — exact-domain match, near-zero FP expectation. Rationale: Anchors on the exact attacker-controlled domain `flipboxstudio.info` named verbatim in the IOC block as both the stage-1 GET endpoint (/payload) and stage-2 POST exfil endpoint (/exfil). The domain is a brand-new typosquat of flipboxstudio.com with no legitimate business use — any hit is high-fidelity.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105 T1568.002 T1041
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel scanner or sandbox detonating the IOC from a corporate egress IP
  • Researcher manually visiting the article and clicking through to the live domain
  • Defensive SOAR playbook auto-fetching the URL for hash extraction
  • Backup/mirror service crawling Composer registry URLs that reference forked IOC repos
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe") and InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("researcher","soar-svc"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify which host(s) resolved/contacted flipboxstudio.info; capture the calling process (InitiatingProcessFileName) — if it is php/php-cli, composer, or a generic shell under a CI runner path, escalate. Pull stage-1 GET vs stage-2 POST distinction from URL path. 2) Contain: sinkhole flipboxstudio.info at DNS/proxy, isolate the host, and immediately rotate every secret accessible to the runner since 2026-05-22 22:32 UTC (GITHUB_TOKEN, fine-grained PATs, AWS/GCP/Azure creds, registry pull tokens). 3) Hunt: pivot the device for /tmp/.laravel_locale/*.php drops, orphan php/ELF processes with ppid=1, and grep composer.lock across the fleet for the imposter SHAs (bba2e443dc7ff1f8704f52a5375383e3f4f643b8 and the others listed in the article).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "flipboxstudio.info"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
( DnsEvents
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where Name has "flipboxstudio.info"
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, ResultCodeName ),
( CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where DestinationHostName has "flipboxstudio.info" or RequestURL has "flipboxstudio.info"
  | project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication ),
( ImDnsActivity
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where DnsQuery has "flipboxstudio.info"
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DnsQuery, DnsResponseCodeName ),
( ImWebSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where Url has "flipboxstudio.info" or HttpHostName has "flipboxstudio.info"
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, Url, HttpMethod, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

PHP CLI drops hidden /tmp dropper artefacts (Laravel-Lang autoload payload) AIInstallation High
Hunts PHP CLI processes (typically from a composer-driven vendor/autoload.php boot) creating files under /tmp/.laravel_locale/<12-hex>.php or /tmp/.<8-hex> matching the exact dropper naming scheme generated by bin2hex(random_bytes(6)) in the malicious src/helpers.php. Combines hidden-path masquerade with the specific php-as-parent shape. Rationale: Anchors on the exact `/tmp/.laravel_locale/<12 hex chars>.php` PHP loader path and `/tmp/.<8 hex chars>` ELF path named in the IOC block, combined with the php-CLI parent shape that follows from `vendor/autoload.php` invoking the malicious helpers.php. The hex-length pattern matches the article's explicit `bin2hex(random_bytes(6))` naming generator.
ATT&CKT1564.001 T1105 T1059.004 T1204.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legit PHP test harness using tempnam('/tmp', '.') for scratch files
  • WP-CLI or a Symfony console command writing locale cache under /tmp
  • PHP-FPM session files when session.save_path is misconfigured to /tmp
  • PHPUnit fixture loader creating hex-named test artefacts in /tmp
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("phpunit","wp-cli","console","artisan") and FolderPath !startswith "/tmp/.laravel_locale")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the file content via EDR quarantine before the dropper self-deletes (~3 second window). Pivot to the parent process tree — confirm the php process was launched from a composer install/update or from a CI runner step rather than from an interactive shell. 2) Contain: kill the php PID and any orphan child (ppid=1) executing from /tmp; isolate the host from network egress; snapshot /tmp before reboot. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC1 (flipboxstudio.info egress) on the same host/timeframe, grep composer.lock for the imposter SHAs (bba2e443..., 26c233e1..., 9ee599d2..., 6b1d5782..., etc.), and rotate every secret in scope on that runner since 2026-05-22 22:32 UTC.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName matches regex @"^php[0-9]?$" or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("php-cli","php-fpm")
| where FolderPath startswith "/tmp/.laravel_locale" 
   or (FolderPath == "/tmp" and FileName matches regex @"^\.[a-f0-9]{6,12}$")
   or (FolderPath startswith "/tmp/." and FileName matches regex @"^[a-f0-9]{6,12}\.php$")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where ActingProcessName matches regex @"/php[0-9]?$" or ActingProcessName endswith "/php-cli"
| where TargetFilePath startswith "/tmp/.laravel_locale/" 
   or TargetFilePath matches regex @"^/tmp/\.[a-f0-9]{6,12}$"
   or TargetFilePath matches regex @"^/tmp/\.[a-f0-9]+/[a-f0-9]{6,12}\.php$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Orphaned process (ppid=1) executing from /tmp hidden hex path (post-dropper stage-2) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts processes reparented to init/systemd (ppid=1) whose image or command-line resolves to /tmp/.<6-12 hex chars> — the exact reparenting + execute-from-deleted-path shape left behind by the Laravel-Lang stage-2 loader after it backgrounds via `php "$f" > /dev/null 2>&1 &` and rm-deletes its own dropper files. Visible in process telemetry even after the file is unlinked. Rationale: Anchors on the article's explicit process IOCs: 'an orphaned php process with ppid=1' and 'an orphaned unnamed ELF process with ppid=1, executing from a now deleted path under /tmp'. Combines the reparent-to-init shape with the /tmp/.<hex> path generated by bin2hex(random_bytes(6)). Survives the self-delete because process metadata is captured at exec time.
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1564.001 T1070.004 T1620
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Containerised PHP daemons in misconfigured images where init=systemd and app binaries live under /tmp
  • CI runner cleanup jobs that detach via nohup and reparent to init
  • Snap-confined apps whose mount squash lands binaries under /tmp/...
  • Custom build agents using mktemp -d in /tmp/.<hex> as a working dir for daemonized helpers
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath startswith "/tmp/snap." or FolderPath startswith "/tmp/.mount_" or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("snapd","systemd-tmpfiles"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: snapshot /proc/<pid>/exe (resolves to the deleted path on Linux even after unlink), /proc/<pid>/environ, /proc/<pid>/maps, and /proc/<pid>/fd before killing — these survive the rm-self-delete and are the highest-fidelity forensic source. Capture all outbound network connections from the PID. 2) Contain: kill the orphan PID and any siblings sharing the same hidden hex base; isolate the host; preserve memory if the host is critical (the binary runs from memory after the on-disk artefact is gone). 3) Hunt: pivot to UC1 (egress to flipboxstudio.info) on the same host, list every consumer of laravel-lang/* packages in the org, rotate every CI secret in scope since 2026-05-22 22:32 UTC, and grep composer.lock fleet-wide for the article's imposter SHAs.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("systemd","init")
| where (FolderPath matches regex @"^/tmp/\.[a-f0-9]{6,12}$")
   or (FileName matches regex @"^php[0-9]?$" and ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"/tmp/\.[a-f0-9]{6,12}(\.php)?")
   or (FolderPath startswith "/tmp/.laravel_locale")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, ProcessId, InitiatingProcessId
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("systemd","init") or ParentProcessId == 1
| where (ActingProcessName matches regex @"^/tmp/\.[a-f0-9]{6,12}$")
   or (ActingProcessName endswith "/php" and ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"/tmp/\.[a-f0-9]{6,12}(\.php)?")
   or (ActingProcessName startswith "/tmp/.laravel_locale")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessId, ActingProcessId
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Orphaned PHP/ELF from /tmp Hidden Hex Path (Laravel-Lang Composer SC Stage-2)
id: 5e2c3d4f-6a7b-8c9d-0e1f-2a3b4c5d6e7f
description: Detects a process whose parent is systemd/init (reparented ppid=1) running from /tmp/.<hex> or whose command line references the Laravel-Lang stage-2 hidden dropper path. The article notes both an orphaned php and an unnamed ELF process executing from a now-deleted /tmp path.
references:
  - https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/laravel-lang-supply-chain-attack
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/23
tags:
  - attack.t1036.005
  - attack.t1564.001
  - attack.t1070.004
  - attack.defense_evasion
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '/systemd'
      - '/init'
  selection_target:
    - Image|re: '^/tmp/\.[a-f0-9]{6,12}$'
    - CommandLine|re: '/tmp/\.[a-f0-9]{6,12}(\.php)?'
    - Image|startswith: '/tmp/.laravel_locale/'
  condition: selection_parent and selection_target
level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE (@process.parent.name:systemd OR @process.parent.name:init OR @process.parent.pid:1) (@process.executable.path:/tmp/.* OR @process.command_line:*/tmp/.*)
(#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 OR #event_simpleName=SyntheticProcessRollup2) ParentBaseFileName=/^(systemd|init)$/i
| (regex("^/tmp/\\.[a-f0-9]{6,12}$", field=ImageFileName) OR regex("/tmp/\\.[a-f0-9]{6,12}(\\.php)?", field=CommandLine) OR regex("^/tmp/\\.laravel_locale/", field=ImageFileName))
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("systemd","init") OR Processes.parent_process_id=1) AND (Processes.process_path="/tmp/.*" OR Processes.process="*/tmp/.*" OR Processes.process_name="php") by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.process_path, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.parent_process_id | `drop_dm_object_name("Processes")` | rex field=process_path "^/tmp/\.(?<hex_name>[a-f0-9]{6,12})$" | rex field=process "/tmp/\.(?<cmd_hex>[a-f0-9]{6,12})" | where isnotnull(hex_name) OR isnotnull(cmd_hex) | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("systemd","init") OR Processes.parent_process_id=1) AND (Processes.process_path="/tmp/.*" OR Processes.process="*/tmp/.*" OR Processes.process_name="php") by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.process_path, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.parent_process_id | `drop_dm_object_name("Processes")` | rex field=process_path "^/tmp/\.(?<hex_name>[a-f0-9]{6,12})$" | rex field=process "/tmp/\.(?<cmd_hex>[a-f0-9]{6,12})" | where isnotnull(hex_name) OR isnotnull(cmd_hex) | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
GitHub bulk git tag force-push by single actor across multiple org repos AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the org-wide tag-rewrite shape that defined the initial-access step: one GitHub actor force-pushing tags across multiple repositories in the same org within a short window (the Laravel-Lang attacker rewrote 502+ tags across four repos in 88 minutes). Combine with commit-author imposter signature 'Your Name' / 'you@example.com'. Rationale: Anchors on the article's exact shape: 'every git tag across multiple popular Composer packages within a single 15 minute window', 502 tags rewritten in one repo, four repos hit in 88 minutes, all by the same compromised credential. The commit-author imposter strings 'Your Name' / 'you@example.com' are also called out verbatim. Sentinel/Defender/Falcon are left empty because GitHub audit telemetry is not in their canonical schemas — Splunk and Datadog (via the GitHub integration) are the realistic shipping paths.
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1078 T1098
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Release engineer rewriting tags during a versioning-scheme migration (e.g. moving from 1.x.x to v1.x.x prefix)
  • Bot account (github-actions[bot], dependabot, release-please) performing org-wide tag housekeeping
  • Repository migration tool replaying tags after import from another VCS
  • Legitimate force-push after revoking an inadvertently-published tag pointing at a leaked secret
Suppression filter
| where actor != "github-actions[bot]" AND actor != "dependabot[bot]" AND actor !="release-please[bot]" AND NOT match(actor, "^.*\[bot\]$")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the actor account and the credential type (PAT, fine-grained PAT, OAuth app, GitHub App, SSH key); pull the actor's recent IP / user-agent history from GitHub audit and compare to known good. Check whether commits in the rewrite carry author identity 'Your Name <you@example.com>' — the campaign signature. 2) Contain: immediately revoke the actor's tokens/sessions and rotate the credential; enable tag protection and disable force-push to tags org-wide; restore tags from a known-good local clone or Packagist mirror SHA. 3) Hunt: search every org repo for commits authored by you@example.com; enumerate every consumer (downstream packages, internal Laravel apps) whose composer.lock points at one of the article's imposter SHAs (a5ea2e8f..., 50ac0db4..., bba2e443..., etc.); treat every CI secret accessible to consumers since 2026-05-22 22:32 UTC as compromised.
source:github (@action:git.push OR @action:git.create) @git.ref:refs/tags/*
CLOUD
index=* sourcetype IN ("github:audit","github_audit_log","github:enterprise:audit") (action="git.push" OR action="git.create" OR action="protected_branch.policy_override") ref="refs/tags/*"
| eval repo_org=mvindex(split(repo,"/"),0)
| stats min(_time) as first_seen max(_time) as last_seen dc(repo) as repo_count dc(ref) as tag_count values(repo) as repos values(ref) as refs by actor, repo_org
| eval window_seconds = last_seen - first_seen
| where tag_count >= 10 AND repo_count >= 2 AND window_seconds <= 3600
| eval window_minutes = round(window_seconds/60, 1)
| convert ctime(first_seen) ctime(last_seen)
| sort - tag_count
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High

Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002

DeviceProcessEvents

| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine

// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"

Shai-Hulud npm worm: postinstall bundle.js spawns TruffleHog secret scan AIInstallation High
Hunts the Shai-Hulud self-replicating npm worm's core payload: a compromised package's postinstall runs bundle.js under node/npm which downloads and executes TruffleHog to harvest GitHub/npm/cloud tokens from the developer machine. Also matches the three known malicious bundle.js SHA-256 hashes. Rationale: Uses the Shai-Hulud campaign's confirmed TTP (bundle.js postinstall executing TruffleHog to steal tokens) plus the three published malicious bundle.js SHA-256 hashes; TruffleHog running under npm/node install is not a legitimate developer workflow. Corroborated across Unit42, ReversingLabs and Beazley. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/npm-supply-chain-attack/ • https://www.reversinglabs.com/blog/shai-hulud-worm-npm • https://checkmarx.com/zero-post/npm-hit-by-shai-hulud-the-self-replicating-supply-chain-attack/ • https://beazley.security/alerts-advisories/malicious-worm-code-found-in-many-npm-packages
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1552.001 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security team intentionally running TruffleHog in a pre-commit hook or CI secret-scan step invoked via npm script
  • Developer manually testing TruffleHog against a local repo
  • A legitimate package that ships a file literally named bundle.js being executed by node (webpack output run standalone)
  • Internal supply-chain research/detonation lab replaying the sample
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("pre-commit","lint-staged","husky") and ProcessCommandLine has "--only-verified")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree on the host — confirm the parent npm/node command and which package's postinstall invoked bundle.js/TruffleHog; capture the SHA-256 and compare to the three known hashes. 2) Contain: isolate the developer machine, revoke and rotate all GitHub/npm/cloud tokens, SSH keys and CI secrets reachable from that host, and freeze the developer's npm publish rights. 3) Hunt: search the fleet for the same package@version in lockfiles, for .github/workflows/shai-hulud.yaml drops (UC2) and for webhook.site exfil beacons (UC3).
union
(DeviceProcessEvents
 | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
 | where (FileName has "trufflehog" or ProcessCommandLine has "trufflehog" or ProcessCommandLine has "bundle.js")
 | where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("node","npm","npx","yarn","pnpm","sh","bash","zsh")
 | extend Evidence="proc_behaviour"
 | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Evidence, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256),
(DeviceFileEvents
 | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
 | where SHA256 in ("b74caeaa75e077c99f7d44f46daaf9796a3be43ecf24f2a1fd381844669da777","dc67467a39b70d1cd4c1f7f7a459b35058163592f4a9e8fb4dffcbba98ef210c","de0e25a3e6c1e1e5998b306b7141b3dc4c0088da9d7bb47c1c00c91e6e4f85d6")
 | extend Evidence="known_bundle_hash", AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName
 | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Evidence, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256)
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (TargetProcessName has "trufflehog" or TargetProcessCommandLine has "trufflehog" or TargetProcessCommandLine has "bundle.js")
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node","npm","npx","yarn","pnpm","sh","bash","zsh")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Shai-Hulud npm worm: malicious GitHub Actions workflow file dropped (.github/workflows/shai-hulud.yaml) AIInstallation High
Hunts the Shai-Hulud worm's persistence/exfil mechanism: writing a rogue GitHub Actions workflow (shai-hulud.yaml / shai-hulud-workflow.yml) into a repo's .github/workflows directory to push captured secrets on every push. This is a filesystem-artifact pivot distinct from the payload-execution UC. Rationale: The exact filenames shai-hulud.yaml / shai-hulud-workflow.yml inside .github/workflows are a signature artifact of this worm confirmed by multiple write-ups; a workflow with this name has no legitimate reason to exist in a repo. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/npm-supply-chain-attack/ • https://cybersecurefox.com/en/shai-hulud-npm-worm-github-actions-supply-chain/ • https://www.zscaler.com/blogs/security-research/mitigating-risks-shai-hulud-npm-worm
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1546 T1567.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security researcher committing a benign workflow file deliberately named shai-hulud.yaml for detection testing
  • A honeypot/canary workflow planted by the blue team
  • Git checkout of a repo that already contains the malicious file being restored during recovery (real compromise, but not a new drop)
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the dropped workflow YAML — confirm it references webhook.site or double-base64 secret dumps and identify the writing process (node/git). 2) Contain: delete the workflow from the repo, disable GitHub Actions for the affected repo, and rotate every secret exposed to that repo's Actions environment. 3) Hunt: correlate the writing host with UC1 (TruffleHog/bundle.js) and UC3 (webhook.site egress); enumerate all repos on that developer's machine for the same file.
DeviceFileEvents
